q-18637.name: Question 1
q-18637.problem: What is the limit of the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{2{n}^{5}-{n}^{2}}{5{n}^{5}-n}$ for $n\ge 1?$
q-18637.worked_solution:
To determine whether the sequence converges or diverges, we need to determine the limit of the sequence as $n$ approaches infinity:

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{2{n}^{5}-{n}^{2}}{5{n}^{5}-n}.
$$

The dominant term in the denominator is $5{n}^{5},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{5}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{2{n}^{5}-{n}^{2}}{5{n}^{5}-n} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{2{n}^{5}}{{n}^{5}}-\frac{{n}^{2}}{{n}^{5}})}{(\frac{5{n}^{5}}{{n}^{5}}-\frac{n}{{n}^{5}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(2-\frac{1}{{n}^{3}})}{(5-\frac{1}{{n}^{4}})} \\  & =\frac{2-0}{5-0} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the limit exists, the sequence converges, and its limit is $\frac{2}{5}.$

q-17568.problem: What is the limit of the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{({n}^{3}-1)({n}^{3}+1)}{{n}^{4}({n}^{2}-2)}$ for $n\ge 1?$
q-17568.worked_solution:
First, we multiply out the numerator and denominator of the sequence and get

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{({n}^{3}-1)({n}^{3}+1)}{{n}^{4}({n}^{2}-2)}=\frac{{n}^{6}-1}{{n}^{6}-2{n}^{4}}.
$$

So to find the limit, we will need to compute

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }⁡{a}_{n}={lim}_{n\to \infty }⁡\frac{{n}^{6}-1}{{n}^{6}-2{n}^{4}}.
$$

The dominant term in the denominator is ${n}^{6},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{6}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }⁡\frac{{n}^{6}-1}{{n}^{6}-2{n}^{4}} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }⁡\frac{(\frac{{n}^{6}}{{n}^{6}}-\frac{1}{{n}^{6}})}{(\frac{{n}^{6}}{{n}^{6}}-\frac{2{n}^{4}}{{n}^{6}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }⁡\frac{(1-\frac{1}{{n}^{6}})}{(1-\frac{2}{{n}^{2}})} \\  & =\frac{1-0}{1-0} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the sequence converges and its limit is $1.$
